rāmāvataraṇakāle nāhamabhūvamityapi hi tasya kālasya anubhavo vaktavyaḥ | āgamāt tatkālajñānamiti cet, āgamo'pi vakturanubhavituranubhavamākṣipati | tadanubhavitrā tāvadbhāvyamiti | nanu vālmīkistāvatā anubhavitā siddhaḥ, na asmādādiḥ | sthāne praśnaḥ, kintu saṃvedanātmano'haṃvimarśasya tāvadiyatā sadbhāvaḥ sadātanaḥ siddhaḥ | saca eka eva paramārthapramātā yadi paraprāṇabuddhipuryaṣṭakaśarīrādayo bhinnāḥ, tadbhedakṛtaśca pramātṛbhedavyavahāra iti tat śarīrādi adyatanaṃ tasmin kāle nābhūdityetadatra tattvam | pralayakāle sṛṣṭimukhārambhe ca na vayaṃ vabhūvimeti, anyathā kālaviśeṣollekho na syāt | vayaṃ na vabhūvimetyapi atra pratītau liṭpratyayāntarnītabhūtakālāvabhāsa unmiṣatyeva | nahi iyaṃ na pratītiḥ | pratītiśca na anubhavarūpā iyaṃ tathātve yogina iva idānīṃ pūrvakālaviṣayasphuṭatāpratyavabhāsaprasaṅgāt | tadiyaṃ smṛtireva bhavantī pūrvānubhavamākṣipatyeva | utprekṣāpi bhavantī smaraṇamanubhavaṃ vā mūlato'valambate, natu andhatamasānupraveśa iva utprekṣā saṃbhavet | kevalaṃ śuddhasaṃvedanamātrasya kāloparāgaśūnyatayā svarūpavyatirekivastvavabhāsāsaṃbhavena ca tadubhayānuprāṇitarūpā smṛtirna saṃbhavatīti śarīrādyuparāgata eva seti | prācyaśarīroparāgaśca (page 65) etaccharīroparāgavibhinna ityevamuparāgadvayasphuṭīkārāyogāt na sphuṭaṃ smṛtitvamatiśiśutāpadānabhūte iva yūnaḥ | anubhavitṛtvena hi yatra abhimāno gāḍhaḥ śarīre, tatraiva aikyasaṃskārābhraṃśādanuvartamānatvena abhimanyamāne sphuṭasmartṛtvābhimāna iti alaṃ bahunā | sthitametat-na ātmano'pūrvatayā prakāśa iti | apūrvatvam iti sattayā | apūrvaprakāśatvam iti adhigamena | atra ca cārtho mantavyaḥ | ata eva vibhajati- naca ātmanaḥ pūrvamasattā, naca sato'pi anubhavaḥ iti | vastutastu sattāpi prakāśaviśrāntaiveti sattāpūrvyaṃ prakāśāpūrvatāyāmeva viśrāmyati,- ityāśayena sāmānādhikaraṇyameva yuktam | pratipadyatām iti cakāro na prayuktaḥ | pramātṛgato'pūrvaprakāśatvavyavahāraḥ prāk pramāturasadbhāve na bhavati pramātṛpramāyattapūrvakālasmaraṇāpekṣatvāt | tadasadbhāve bhavanasya vy
**The eternal knower: "I was never not"** Memory seems to bind the self to the past — to what the self has itself experienced. But then the objection arises, and it is a sharp one. "I was not at the time of the Rāmāyaṇa," the reader says. "Vālmīki composed it long ago, and I was not there to experience it; so how can the self, which remembers only what it has experienced, be the eternal knower?" Abhinavagupta answers that the objection mistakes the body for the self. It is true that *this body* was not at the time of the Rāmāyaṇa — but that is not the self. The "I"-recollection, the aham-vimarśa, is of the consciousness-nature, and it is eternal. And here is the crucial move: if memory reaches only what has been experienced, then even the Vālmīki of the Rāmāyaṇa was an experiencer; and the āgama itself, by which we learn of that time, presupposes an experiencer. What flashes in the "we were not" — the past-time-appearance, in the perfect tense — is itself a cognition; and since it is not the experience-form (else the past would flash like the yogin's present), it must be memory. And memory, by its very nature, presupposes a prior experience. So every memory, even the memory of the Rāmāyaṇa, points back to an experiencer who was there. This is where the eternal knower enters. The pure consciousness-mere, being free of the tint of time, cannot by itself bear the memory; the memory is of the body-and-the-rest-tinted. But the tint of the prior body is distinct from the tint of this body — so the memory-ness, if pinned to the body, would not be clear (as the young man who was never a child would have no clear memory of childhood). The clear memory requires the firm conceit of the experiencer — and that conceit, in its root, is the self that was there. And that self, being consciousness, is not cut by time. So the manifestation of the self is not un-precedented (apūrva). It does not begin to shine at some moment; it was always shining. The being-ness of the self rests in its manifestation, and its being was never otherwise. Hence the "un-precedented manifestation" (apūrva-prakāśa) that we seem to see — the new appearance of things in time — presupposes, and rests upon, the eternal knower. The body's appearance is un-precedented, but only against the background of the eternal, always-manifested param-essence knower. And that knower is the param-eśvara, who is never un-precedented in his manifestation; and all the knowers are un-divided from him. So, in truth, there is no un-precedented manifestation at all. This is the point of the Gītā verse that Abhinavagupta cites: "For truly I was never not… nor shall we not be." The self — the param-essence knower — is un-cut by all three times: past, present, and future. It did not come into being, and it will not pass away. And because all the knowers are one with it, the same is true, in the deepest sense, of them all. The un-precedented manifestation may appear in the māyā-bound knower, but it rests in the eternal knower. The pramāṇa — the valid means by which we know — is thus grounded, in the end, in this one eternal knower, who was never not, and who is the self of all. ---

> The upoddhāta's third kārikā makes the memory-argument for the eternal self. Memory reaches what one > has experienced; but if the self were momentary (as the kṣaṇikavāda holds), no experience could be > carried across moments to be remembered, and memory would be impossible. The fact that memory occurs — > that I can re-appropriate a past experience as mine — shows there is a self that persists through the > change of moments. The argument is the same as in the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi: memory presupposes a > persisting recognizer, and that recognizer is the non-inert self.
